operations.evidence: Ratings concern trend reliability; they do not validate individual incidents.
The review engaged a sample of nine police forces; it also consulted HMICFRS Home Office ONS and wider stakeholders; OSR cautioned that findings may not generalise to all forces.
Sample evidence is not a census; review conclusions need scope metadata.
Seven different crime-recording IT systems were in use; some forces used different versions of the same system; system variation is a barrier to standardisation.
System inventory can change; system identity alone does not quantify record error.
Crime-recording system changes can harm data quality; changes can disrupt data sent to the Home Office; supplier dependence can delay or increase the cost of fixes.
Risk differs by force and supplier; not every migration causes an error.
Internal audit stages were broadly similar; record checking and validation standards varied; operational priorities resources and IT systems shape QA arrangements.
Broad similarity does not prove equivalent assurance; force-specific evidence is required.
Home Office QA cannot determine whether the right crime was recorded; record-level accuracy requires audit of crime records; HMICFRS performs that audit function.
Administrative validation and accuracy audit are different; inspection intervals create information gaps.
ONS is two steps removed from police-force record-level data; ONS relies on Home Office collation and QA; without record-level access ONS checks are largely consistency based.
Published aggregate consistency is not record-level accuracy; quality claims must reflect dependency.
The quality review is a step toward possible reaccreditation; critical recommendations must be addressed first; OSR will decide reassessment readiness after sufficient improvement.
Reaccreditation is not automatic; current official-statistics status must be preserved.
NDQIS targets flagged collections; examples include knife crime domestic abuse and online crime; computer-assisted classification has been used to improve consistency.
Tools apply to defined collections; tool output is not direct parcel evidence.
ONS should publish and update NDQIS developments; methods should be documented; strengths and limitations of tools should be communicated.
Programme existence does not prove all actions complete; tool versions require dates.
The Data Foundations stream proposed a national data quality framework; it proposed a national data quality register; it proposed a model for data quality targets.
Recommendations are not confirmed implementation; maturity varies by force.
PND has provided quarterly force data-quality assessments since 2019; the process runs more than 50 validation and logic checks; checks cover multiple quality dimensions.
PND assessment is distinct from crime-statistics production QA; force engagement is not compulsory.
PND checks include accuracy validity completeness and uniqueness; checks are weighted and combined; the overall score is out of 100.
The score is not a parcel safety score; weights and process version must be retained.
PND focuses largely on person and location data; the process differs from Data Hub reconciliation; direct impact on published crime-count statistics can be limited.
Indirect quality improvements are possible; the two processes must not be merged.
Some forces provide only dates for stop and search; date-only records can appear at midnight; datetime precision varies by force.
Midnight concentration may be an artefact; time-of-day analysis requires precision checks.
Outcome false means nothing was found; an empty outcome means no outcome was provided; outcome-linked-to-object can be null when not provided.
False empty and null are not equivalent; missing states must not be converted to zero.
